units.translation: And from their eyes they shed a hateful stream.
For the sleeping mind is brightened by the eyes.
There is a wonder before my eyes.
I love the eyes of Persuasion.
from a calm eye
May he be seen with a kindly eye.
Indeed, one must go into the depths with a seeing eye.
the prow, looking ahead with its eyes on the path
Do not love violence, seeing it with just eyes.
Take yourself out of my sight as quickly as possible.
She sent the eye-charming arrow.
casting aside the left eye
O delightful eye, having four parts for me,
and overseers of ancestral eyes
For I consider the eye of the house to be the master's presence.
For the eye of all the land of Theseus would come.
until it took away the eye of dark night,
but when the eye of gloomy night comes,
the starry eye of Leto's daughter.

ὅμοια [like things] adverbially for ὁμοίως [likewise], equally.

[The ancient Attics pronounced ὁμοῖος [like], as also ἐρῆμος [deserted] and ἑτοῖμος [ready], about which we have spoken in their proper places. In M it is consistently ὅμοιος [like]. Apollonius on pronouns p. 63 (323): οὐκ ἐξωμάλισται τὰ τῶν διαλέκτων, μάλιστα δὲ τὰ τῶν Ἀττικῶν. ὅμοιος καὶ γέλοιος προπαροξύνοντές φασιν, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκέτι τὰ τούτοις παραπλήσια [the dialectal forms are not uniform, especially those of the Attics. They say ὅμοιος and γέλοιος with the accent on the antepenult, but no longer the words similar to these]. He seems to call the later Attics those to whom the Homeric scholiast on Il. 14, 521 and Etym. M. p. 224, 42 assign this accent. ὁμοῖος [like] was approved by Herodian vol. 1 p. 137, 14, where see Lentz's note. Eustathius treated this question more often; see him at p. 206, 13. 531, 45. 569, 18. 799, 40. 1817, 15.]
(thus Canterus for βλάβας [harms]) λαβεῖν [to take],

where Weilius seems rightly to have deleted λαβεῖν [to take], inserting αὐτός [himself] after ὁμοίας [like], for which the scholiast put ού, ἢ τὴν δίκην συμμαχοῦσαν ἡμῖν κατ᾿ αὐτῶν πέμψον, ἢ σὺ κόλασον αὐτούς [either send Justice fighting on our side against them, or punish them yourself]. Suidas noted the expression taken from the wrestling-school ὁμοίας λαβάς [like grips], instead of μεταλήψεις καὶ ἀντιμεταθέσεις [changes and exchanges].

where the scholiast says: ἔθος γὰρ τούτοις, ὅταν πέσωσιν ὁμοῦ, ὡς μηδένα ἐπιπεσεῖν τοῦ λοιποῦ, πάλιν ἐγερθέντας ἐφ᾽ ὁμοίω συμπλεκῆναι σχήματι, ὅπερ τὴν αὐτὴν εἶπε λαβήν [for it is their custom, when they fall together, so that no one falls upon the other for the rest, to get up again and grapple in the same posture, which he called the same grip].
